title: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent place over $35 billion worth of Nvidia chip orders
author: B
text:
S

soAsian
Well-known member

ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have ordered Nvidia graphics cards carrying a combined potential value exceeding $35 billion, Reuters reported October 20, citing unnamed sources. The requests cover more than three million RTX PRO 5500 cards, an export-compliant workstation product. Nvidia reportedly cannot guarantee fulfillment because demand exceeds planned supply. The companies primarily intend to use the cards for AI inference, the operation of already trained models. These are reported orders at sticker prices, not completed sales or recognized revenue.

The significance extends beyond the headline amount. The reported purchasing effort suggests that access to usable computing capacity remains a strategic priority for China’s largest internet companies. Their challenge is securing hardware that can support expanding services within regulatory and supply constraints.

Inference makes this particularly consequential. Building a model attracts attention, but serving users creates recurring computing requirements. Chatbots, recommendation systems, coding assistants, and enterprise applications must generate responses continuously. Limited hardware availability could therefore affect operating costs, deployment schedules, and the number of customers a service can support.

For buyers, the practical calculation involves more than GPU purchase prices. Engineering teams must evaluate memory capacity, energy consumption, software compatibility, networking, and performance on their actual workloads. A legally available processor can still prove expensive if deploying it requires additional systems or extensive optimization.

For Nvidia, large requests indicate commercial interest without establishing deliverable business. Production allocation, customer acceptance, and regulatory conditions determine how much demand ultimately becomes revenue. Treating the entire reported amount as secured sales would overstate certainty.

The broader lesson concerns industrial policy. Restrictions can redirect purchasing toward alternative products and suppliers while encouraging buyers to redesign their infrastructure strategies. They also make procurement resilience more important.

What matters now is execution: which orders ship, what useful computing capacity they deliver, and whether that capacity supports commercially sustainable AI services.
